du=∂u∂x dx, \mathrm { d } u = \frac { \partial u } { \partial x } \, \mathrm { d } x ,du=∂x∂u​dx,

∂u∂x=dudx. \frac { \partial u } { \partial x } = \frac { \mathrm { d } u } { \mathrm { d } x } .∂x∂u​=dxdu​.

so

∂2u∂x2=d2u∧d2xdx∧d2x. \frac { \partial ^ 2 u } { \partial x ^ 2 } = \frac { \mathrm { d } ^ 2 u \wedge \mathrm { d } ^ 2 x } { \mathrm { d } x \wedge \mathrm { d } ^ 2 x } .∂x2∂2u​=dx∧d2xd2u∧d2x​.

Now suppose that u u u is a function of x x x and y y y. Then

du=∂u∂x dx+∂u∂y dy, \mathrm { d } u = \frac { \partial u } { \partial x } \, \mathrm { d } x + \frac { \partial u } { \partial y } \, \mathrm { d } y ,du=∂x∂u​dx+∂y∂u​dy,

so

so

Thus,

∂2u∂x2=∂(∂u∂x)∂x=d(du∧dydx∧dy)∧dydx∧dy, \frac { \partial ^ 2 u } { \partial x ^ 2 } = \frac { \partial \left ( \frac { \partial u } { \partial x } \right ) } { \partial x } = \frac { \mathrm { d } \left ( \frac { \mathrm { d } u \wedge \mathrm { d } y } { \mathrm { d } x \wedge \mathrm { d } y } \right ) \wedge \mathrm { d } y } { \mathrm { d } x \wedge \mathrm { d } y } ,∂x2∂2u​=∂x∂(∂x∂u​)​=dx∧dyd(dx∧dydu∧dy​)∧dy​,

On the other hand,

#100 Re #87:

The coefficients appearing here are those that appear in Bell polynomials, and they are well known (although not by me, until yesterday) both to come from counting partitions and to give a formula for the higher derivatives of a composite function, Faà di Bruno's formula. This formula gives the higher cojet differentials of f(x)f(x)f(x), where fff is a real-valued function of a real variable, differentiable at least nnn times, and xxx is a real-valued quantity (technically a real-valued function on some manifold), also differentiable at least nnn times:

dn(f(x))=∑πf(∣π∣)(x)∏B∈πd∣B∣x, \mathrm{d}^n\big(f(x)\big) = \sum_\pi f^{({|\pi|})}(x) \prod_{B\in{\pi}} \mathrm{d}^{|B|}x ,dn(f(x))=π∑​f(∣π∣)(x)B∈π∏​d∣B∣x,

where the sum is taken over the set of all partitions of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n}, each partition π\piπ being thought of as a subset of the powerset of {1,…,n}\{1,\ldots,n\}{1,…,n} (so that both π\piπ and any B∈πB \in \piB∈π have a cardinality given by ∣⋅∣{|{\cdot}|}∣⋅∣).

A partly multivariable version of the formula may be adapted to coflare forms. First some notation: if A={i1,i2,…,in}A = \{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_n\}A={i1​,i2​,…,in​} is a finite multisubset of N\mathbb{N}N, then write dAu\mathrm{d}^A{u}dAu for di1di2⋯dinu\mathrm{d}_{i_1}\mathrm{d}_{i_2}{\cdots}\mathrm{d}_{i_n}udi1​​di2​​⋯din​​u (which is unambiguously defined if uuu is at least nnn times differentiable). Also, if B⊆{1,…,n}B \subseteq \{1,\ldots,n\}B⊆{1,…,n} (a set, not any multiset), then let iBi_BiB​ be {ij  ∣  j∈B}\{i_j \;|\; j \in B\}{ij​∣j∈B} (a multiset). With this notation,

dA(f(x))=∑πf(∣π∣)(x)∏B∈πdiBx, \mathrm{d}^A\big(f(x)\big) = \sum_\pi f^{({|\pi|})}(x) \prod_{B\in{\pi}} \mathrm{d}^{i_B}x ,dA(f(x))=π∑​f(∣π∣)(x)B∈π∏​diB​x,

a partial decategorification of the cojet version.

A fully multivariable version of the formula would also allow fff to be a function of mmm variables, with d(f(x1,…,xm))=∇f(x1,…,xm)⋅⟨dx1,…,dxm⟩=∑j=1mDjf(x1,…,xm)dxj\mathrm{d}\big(f(x_1,\ldots,x_m)\big) = \nabla{f}(x_1,\ldots,x_m) \cdot \langle{\mathrm{d}x_1,\ldots,\mathrm{d}x_m}\rangle = \sum_{j=1}^m \mathrm{D}_j{f}(x_1,\ldots,x_m) \mathrm{d}x_jd(f(x1​,…,xm​))=∇f(x1​,…,xm​)⋅⟨dx1​,…,dxm​⟩=∑j=1m​Dj​f(x1​,…,xm​)dxj​ as the order-111 case, but I haven't tried to think that through yet.

ETA: You can take AAA and iBi_BiB​ to be tuples rather than multisets, if you prefer. But the order doesn't matter, just as with partial derivatives.

content: #101 Someone wrote a paper containing our work on the correct way to understand second derivatives, later than us but probably independently of us: Extending the Algebraic Manipulability of Differentials by Bartlett and Khurshudyan. Note that they also have an application at the end to solving some second-order differential equations.
subject: What is a variable?

content: #102 Actually, the most interesting part of that paper is not the application near the end but the historical discussion at the very end, showing how this stuff was known to Leibniz and Euler before it was forgotten.
